1:
Exactly what is being blamed is set out carefully by Keil and Delitzsch, and it is narrower than the verse looks. The clause about the daughter of Pharaoh cannot mean, as earlier commentators supposed, and especially the daughter of Pharaoh, but means along with her; she is thereby distinguished from the foreign wives who turned Solomon's heart away, so that the blame pronounced upon those marriages does not attach to that one. What is blamed is only this, that against the law he loved many foreign wives, and wives of nations with which Israel was not to intermarry — the express prohibition having covered the Canaanite women alone. Ellicott sorts the five nations the same way: the first three were kindred to Israel, of the stock of Abraham, and now among Solomon's subjects, while the last two were of the old Canaanitish stock and now inferior allies. To the last alone the prohibition of the Law properly attached; but the reason on which it was grounded applied equally to the others, since they too had fallen into the worship of false gods, and the extension was recognised by the Jews after the captivity. He notes as well that no Egyptian idolatry is anywhere mentioned.

Clarke will not let the Egyptian marriage off so lightly, holding that she was also one of the strange women and an idolater; many think she became a proselyte to the Jewish religion, he says, but of this there is no evidence. Gill puts the charge in a word, that the love was a lustful and not a lawful one, and of women who were not only of foreign countries but not his lawful wives.

Henry treats the whole chapter as a fall and asks how it could happen. This is a sad story, and very surprising: shall Solomon fall, that was the beauty of Israel and so great a blessing of his generation? Yes, and the Scripture is faithful in relating it, and in referring to it long after. The beginning of it, he says, was that Solomon gave himself to women, the very thing his mother had particularly cautioned him against, and that his father's own fall had begun with the lusts of the flesh, which he should have taken warning by. Out of that Henry draws the rule he is really after: lesser sins made bold with open the door to greater. David had multiplied wives too much, and perhaps that made Solomon presume it lawful; those in reputation for religion know not what mischief a bad example may do, particularly to their own children, and one bad act of a good man may be of more pernicious consequence than twenty of a wicked man. Probably Solomon, when he began to multiply wives, did not intend to exceed his father's number — but the way of sin is down-hill, and those who have got into it cannot easily stop themselves.
3:
The thousand is read by three witnesses as a total rather than a household. Keil and Delitzsch call the figures round numbers, approximating to the reality, and hold that they are not to be understood as all present at once but as including every woman received into the harem during the whole of his reign, whereas the threescore queens and fourscore concubines named in another book are to be understood as present at court at one time. Ellicott says the same of the institution — the harem of an Eastern king is simply an adjunct of his magnificence, and the relation of the wives to him little more than nominal — and then presses further than the others dare. The numbers, though found also in the old Greek version and in Josephus, are not only extraordinarily large but excessive by comparison with the other account, and disproportionate in the relative number of the superior and the inferior wives; it is possible, he concludes, that the text may be corrupt, though the corruption must then be of ancient date. Gill calls the number prodigious and suggests that these might not all be for use but for state, after the manner of the eastern monarchs.

Clarke raises a practical difficulty and then refuses every excuse built on it. How Solomon could get so many of the blood royal from the different surrounding nations is astonishing, though probably the daughters of noblemen and generals are included; and the concubines he explains as wives of the second rank, taken according to the usages of those times, whose offspring could not inherit, standing to Solomon as Hagar and Keturah did to Abraham. Then the refusal. Was it possible that such a person could have any piety to God, who was absorbed by such a number of women? We scarcely allow a man to have the fear of God who has a second wife or mistress; in what state then must the man be who has a thousand of them? We may endeavour to excuse all this, Clarke grants, by saying that it was a custom in the East, and that there were many of these women whom Solomon probably never saw — but was there any of them whom he might not have seen? And how then is it said that he loved many strange women, that he clave to them in love? He ends on the rule he wants remembered: as we should not condemn what God justifies, so we should not justify what God condemns.
4:
That the collapse came late is itself part of the charge. Gill puts Solomon near sixty at the time, reckoning from the age of the son who succeeded him, and takes the lateness as an aggravation, that in his old age, when by long experience he might have been thought still wiser and less lustful, this was what he came to. Keil and Delitzsch describe the same season as one in which the flesh gained the supremacy over the spirit, so that his heart was no longer wholly with the Lord — the word meaning entirely devoted, as the heart of David his father had been, who had indeed grievously sinned but had not fallen into idolatry. Ellicott reads the implication as senile feebleness, possibly the premature result of a life of indulgence, since Solomon could not have been very old if he was but a child at his accession.

What kind of apostasy it was is Ellicott's real subject, and his answer is not the obvious one. It is not at all likely that Solomon forsook the worship of God; his idolatry was rather an inclination to an eclectic adoption of various forms of faith and worship, as simply various phases of reverence to the One Supreme Power, each having its own peculiar significance and beauty. Such a spirit, holding itself superior to the old laws and principles of the faith of Israel, he calls the natural fruit of an overweening confidence in his own wisdom — the philosophic spirit, holding no creed but contemplating and condescending to all. Whatever it may have owed to the baser female influence, it seems to Ellicott likelier to have been the demoralising effect of an absolutely despotic power, of a world-wide fame for wisdom, and of an over-luxurious magnificence. He offers two further suggestions in the same vein: that it may have had a kind of harmony with the weary and hopeless conviction that all things are vanity, since there is something of kinship between the belief that all worships are true and the belief that all are false; and that it may have been thought good policy to conciliate the subject races by doing honour to their religions, much as the Roman Empire delighted to do when faith in its own religion had died out.
5:
How far Solomon actually went is a question the witnesses answer differently, and Keil and Delitzsch answer it most cautiously. The idolatry condemned here, they say, consisted in his building altars to the deities of all his foreign wives, upon which those wives offered incense and sacrifice to their idols; it is not stated that he himself also offered sacrifice to them. But they will not let the distinction excuse him: even the building of altars for idols was a participation in idolatry irreconcilable with true fidelity to the Lord. Clarke takes the harder line and says outright that he burnt incense to them himself, and that he seems to have gone as far in iniquity as it was possible.

On who these gods were, both commentators reach for comparative religion. Keil and Delitzsch make Astarte the chief female deity of all the Canaanitish tribes, note that her worship was transplanted from Tyre to Carthage where it flourished greatly, and identify her as a moon-goddess whom the Greeks and Romans called sometimes Aphrodite and sometimes Urania or Juno. Ellicott adds a derivation, that the name may come from a root found in both Syriac and Persian which became the Greek and Latin words for a star, and points to the ancient name of a city in Bashan meaning the horned Ashteroth; he observes that this is the first place where the name is used in the singular and expressly limited to the goddess of the Zidonians, whereas the earlier history speaks of the Ashtaroth in the plural alongside the Baalim, perhaps meaning simply the gods and goddesses of idolatry in general. Of the worship itself he says only that it was one of chartered license and impurity.

On the second name the two part company. Keil and Delitzsch insist that Milcom must not be confounded with the Molech of the early Canaanites, to whom children were offered. Ellicott holds the opposite, that Milcom is probably only a variety of the well-known Molech, which is actually used for it two verses later; the name, he argues, is a general title signifying only king, as Baal signifies lord, and might be applied to the supreme god of any idolatrous system — which is why the same horrible rite of passing children through the fire is forbidden as a Canaanite practice and is also recorded of the Carthaginians in times of great national calamity. Gill contributes the local connection instead, that Solomon was enticed by the Zidonian women he had, and that according to the Phoenician histories he married a daughter of Hiram king of Tyre and Zidon; Ashtoreth he identifies flatly with the Venus of the Greeks, citing an ancient writer who says the Sidonians had a temple of Astarte and took her for the moon.
6:
Where the high places stood is agreed and pointedly described. Gill has Solomon order the building, or at least suffer it to be built, at the instigation of his Moabitish women, on the hill before Jerusalem — the mount of Olives, he says, called from this afterwards the mount of corruption. Clarke identifies the hill in five words to the same effect. Ellicott adds what the siting meant: it was on the mount of Olives, part of which still traditionally bears the name of the Mount of Offence, facing and rivalling the Temple on the opposite height; and he locates the place of actual sacrifice to Molech separately, in the valley of the son of Hinnom, east or south-east of the city and not far from the foot of the mountain.

How many altars were needed is a question Keil and Delitzsch answer by arithmetic rather than by the text. When it is said that he did likewise for all his foreign wives, what is meant is that he built altars for their gods; and three altars, which are named together only in the fuller account in another book, were sufficient for all of them. For the Hittites and the Edomites do not appear to have had any deities peculiar to themselves: the Hittites no doubt worshipped Astarte in common with the Sidonians, and the Edomites probably worshipped Milcom. In the whole of the Old Testament, they note, there is only one place where gods of the Edomites are mentioned at all, and there no names are given.

Why the building did not stop at one is Gill's contribution, and it is a point about court politics rather than religion: when Solomon had done it for one wife he could not refuse it to another without greatly disobliging her, and so it went on for as many of them as asked. On the summary judgement of the passage the witnesses are brief and united. Gill glosses the doing of evil in the sight of the Lord by saying that idolatry is what it names, and that nothing is more provoking to him; Keil and Delitzsch let the comparison in the verse stand as it is, that he went not fully after the Lord as did David his father.
9:
That God had appeared to him twice is the first thing every witness fastens on. Ellicott observes that stress is laid on these direct visions precisely because they contrast with the usual indirect revelation through the prophets, and so carried with them peculiar privilege and responsibility. Keil and Delitzsch put the same emphasis where an early commentator put it, that God had appeared for the purpose of warning him himself and had not merely caused him to be warned by prophets. Henry turns it into the first of two counts against Solomon, the most base ingratitude that could be: he turned from the Lord who had appeared to him twice, once before he began to build the temple and once after he had dedicated it. God keeps account of the gracious visits he makes us, Henry adds, whether we do or no, and will remember it against us if we turn from him.

Clarke pauses to say why the record of the fall had to be made at all. Had not this man's delinquency been strongly marked by the divine disapprobation, it would have had a fatal effect on the morals of mankind; vice is vice, no matter who commits it, and God is as much displeased with sin in Solomon as he can be with it in the most profligate and uneducated wretch.

He then draws a distinction between the guilt of an act and the desert of the man who commits it. God sees the same sin in precisely the same degree of moral turpitude as to the act itself, yet circumstances may greatly aggravate the offence and subject the offender to greater punishment. Solomon was wise and knew better; his understanding showed him the vanity as well as the wickedness of idolatry; God had appeared to him twice and so given him the most direct proof of his being and of his providence; and the promises had been fulfilled in a manner proving that they came by a divine counsel and not by any kind of casualty. Hence Clarke's conclusion, which is the sharp end of the whole argument: Solomon deserved more punishment for his worship of Ashtaroth than any of the Sidonians did, though they performed precisely the same acts, because the Sidonians had never known the true God and Solomon had been fully acquainted with him. Henry reaches the second count by the same road, the most wilful disobedience, since this was the very thing concerning which God had expressly commanded him; and he generalises it, that those who have dominion over men are apt to forget God's dominion over them, and while they demand obedience from their inferiors to deny it to him who is the Supreme. Gill states the aggravation more plainly still, that the command had been particularly given to Solomon and he had been warned to observe it.
11:
How the sentence reached Solomon is not stated in the verse, and both Gill and Keil and Delitzsch supply the same answer: not in a vision as before, but through a prophet, and probably Ahijah the Shilonite, who appears later in the chapter. Clarke reads the message itself as one more opening rather than a closing: was not this another warning from the Lord, and might not Solomon have yet recovered himself? Was there not mercy in this message which he might have sought and found?

Henry finds the sentence exactly fitted to the crime. Since Solomon had revolted from God, part of his kingdom should revolt from his family; he had given God's glory to the creature, and therefore God would give his crown to his servant, who should bear rule over much of what Solomon had laboured for. This was a great mortification, Henry adds, to a man who had pleased himself with the prospect of entailing his rich kingdom upon his heirs for ever — and he draws the general lesson that sin brings ruin upon families, cuts off entails, alienates estates, and lays men's honour in the dust. Keil and Delitzsch set out the shape of the threat with its two limitations: the kingdom shall be torn away and given to a servant, yet not in Solomon's lifetime for his father's sake, and not the whole of it, since one tribe shall remain to his son.

On what those two reservations rest, Gill is careful to say that the sparing is not for the merits of David but for the promises made to him. Clarke sees a longer purpose running through both. The line of the Messiah had to be preserved, so that not only the tribe but the regal line and the regal right had to be kept, and all of it for the true David's sake; and as David was a type of the Messiah, so Jerusalem was a type of the true Church, which is why the old Jerusalem had to be preserved in the hands of that tribe until the true David should establish the New Jerusalem in the same land and the same city. What a series of providences, Clarke exclaims, it required to do all these things.
14:
The adversaries are read by every witness as chastisement rather than misfortune. Gill states the arrangement plainly: though God did not take the kingdom from Solomon for his sin, he chastised him with the rod of men as he had said he would, suffering one and then another to rise up and disturb his peace in his old age. Clarke plays on the Hebrew word for adversary and gets a whole biography out of it — when Solomon sent to Hiram for help in building the temple he could say there was no satan and all his kingdom was at peace, every man under his vine and fig tree, but now that he had turned away from God three satans rise up against him. Henry makes the same point by measuring the men against the king: these two were inconsiderable and could not have done anything worth taking notice of if Solomon had not first made God his enemy. What hurt could they have done to so great and powerful a king, he asks, if he had not by sin made himself mean and weak? If God be on our side we need not fear the greatest adversary; but if he be against us he can make us fear the least, and the very grasshopper shall be a burden.

Henry adds two observations that govern the rest of the chapter. The first is that God stirred both of them up: though they themselves were moved by principles of ambition or revenge, he made use of them to serve his design of correcting Solomon, deferring the principal judgement while making him feel the smart of the rod for his greater humiliation — so that whoever are in any way adversaries to us, we must take notice of the hand of God stirring them up, as he bade Shimei curse David, and look through the instruments of our trouble to the author of it. The second is that both enmities had their origin in David's time and in his conquests of the two countries, so that Solomon inherited his father's quarrels along with his father's enlarged dominion and increased treasure.

Who Hadad was is settled from the name. Ellicott calls it a title rather than a name, most frequently found as a designation of the kings of Syria though here given to a member of the royal family of Edom, and reports the ancient authorities who make it a Syriac title of the sun — in that respect like the more celebrated title Pharaoh — assumed by the king either as indicating descent from the sun-god or simply as an appellation of splendour and majesty. Keil and Delitzsch note that the same name was borne by a pre-Mosaic king of Edom, which shows it was not uncommon in that royal house, and refuse the conjecture that this Hadad was that king's grandson, since it rests on the false assumption that the earlier king reigned in David's day.

The war he fled from is described most fully by Ellicott, and the other accounts do not quite agree with this one. It is noted elsewhere in close connection with the great struggle with the Syrians, with the victory ascribed in one record to Joab and in another to Abishai, while here David himself takes part, perhaps completing a conquest that Joab had successfully begun. What is not in doubt is the character of it: a war of ruthless extermination of every male except those who fled the country or found refuge in its rocky fastnesses, carried on by systematic ravage under Joab's command, and how it was provoked we do not know. Clarke reckons that Joab exterminated all the males in the course of six months, and notes an old version which reads not that he went up to bury the slain but to take the spoils of the slain.
17:
How old the fugitive was is a point Clarke will not let the English obscure. The words mean a little boy, he says, one who was apprehensive of his danger and could with his father's servants make his escape — not an infant. Gill fixes the moment of the flight against the previous verse, that Hadad got away while Joab was burying the slain, and so came clear of the general slaughter of the males.

The route is traced stage by stage. Clarke has them retire first to Midian, and then, not supposing themselves safe there, go on to Paran in the south of Idumea, where they gathered a number of persons to join them before going straight to Egypt. Ellicott stops on the oddity of the first stage: we should have expected the starting-point of the flight to be described in Edom itself, so that the reference must be either to some branch of the Midianitish tribes settled between Edom and the desert, or to a city of that name near the Gulf of Elath which certain ancient authorities mention and to which the old Greek version expressly refers here. Paran he identifies as part of the Sinaitic region, west of the Edomite territory and evidently inhabited at that time by an independent race, from which the fugitives enlisted support. Keil and Delitzsch explain what that support was for: from Paran they took men with them as guides through the desert.

The reception in Egypt is described as a full settlement rather than a refuge. Keil and Delitzsch have Pharaoh give them a house and maintenance and assign Hadad land to cultivate for the support of the fugitives who had come with him. Ellicott asks which Pharaoh this was and answers that chronological considerations, and perhaps internal probabilities, suggest he was not the king who became father-in-law to Solomon, though the same policy of alliance with the occupants of Palestine and the neighbourhood is exemplified in both cases; jealousy of the growing power of Israel under David and Solomon, he suggests, might well prompt this favourable reception of Hadad, as it afterwards prompted the reception of Jeroboam.
19:
The favour Hadad found is described as an adoption rather than a kindness. Keil and Delitzsch have Pharaoh give him the sister of his own wife to wife, and the son born of that marriage weaned in the royal palace and then brought up among the sons of Pharaoh. Ellicott presses on the two proper names and finds nothing behind either: the queen's name is unknown, either in history or in the Egyptian monuments, and the son's is similarly unknown; but the weaning in the house of Pharaoh, no doubt with the customary festival, indicated the admittance of the child into the royal family of Egypt. Gill supplies a reason for the favour from the man himself, his comely personage and princely qualities and good behaviour as he grew up, and reads the son's name for its meaning, that it signifies stealth and may have been given in memory of Hadad's own being carried away by stealth out of his land.

The request to leave turns on a piece of news and a silence. Gill notes that the death of princes is soon known in other countries, and especially of a king of such fame as David. Keil and Delitzsch treat Pharaoh's question — what is there lacking to thee with me? — as a pure expression of love and attachment which involved the request that he would remain, and print the exchange whole, with Hadad's answer that he lacked nothing, howbeit let him go in any wise — a denial that concedes the kindness and asks release regardless — and they note that we are not told Pharaoh granted it, though the release must be supplied. Gill spreads the question out into its parts, whether anything was lacking of an equipage suitable to his birth and marriage, or of provisions for his household, or of honour and respect, or of any favour at all. Clarke marks what Hadad did not say: it does not appear that he avowed his real intention to Pharaoh, for at this time there must have been peace between Israel and Egypt, Solomon having married the daughter of Pharaoh.
23:
The second adversary comes from the opposite quarter, as Gill observes in half a line: one from the north, as the other was from the south. Clarke reads both of them as the exact fulfilment of an older threat, that if he commit iniquity I will chasten him with the rod of men and with the stripes of the children of men, spoken by the prophet Nathan. Ellicott takes up the name and finds a pattern in it: Rezon appears to signify prince, which might naturally mark the founder of a new power, and a king of Damascus named later would belong to this generation and may be the same man. He also reports the tradition Josephus quotes from Nicolaus of Damascus, that for ten generations from the days of David all the kings of Syria bore the name of Hadad, and judges it to mean only that Hadad was the official title of the monarchy.

How Rezon rose is told slightly differently by the two who tell it. Keil and Delitzsch have him flee from his lord the king of Zobah for some reason not assigned, probably while that king was at war with David and before his complete overthrow, collect a company from the fugitives, and afterwards march on Damascus, take possession of the city and make himself king there — which they think did not happen until towards the close of David's reign or even after his death. Clarke makes him one of the captains of that king, escaping with his men after the defeat, living as is supposed by plunder, seizing Damascus and reigning there until David took the city and drove him out, and then recovering it after Solomon's defection, when he found that God had departed from Israel. Clarke adds that some think Hadad and Rezon were the same person. Ellicott supports the later dating from the record of the war: at that time David put governors in Damascus and reduced its inhabitants to a tributary condition, so that an independent power there probably dates only from the later days of Solomon, though there may have been some rising earlier in the reign.

The closing clause is where Ellicott registers a difficulty in the text itself. The recurrence to Hadad in the phrase about the mischief he did is curiously abrupt as it stands, and the reading is doubtful: if the general reading of the old Greek version is taken, then Edom must be substituted for Syria, which involves only a slight change in the Hebrew; if the explanation given by Josephus is correct, the received text must stand. Gill limits the other phrase in the verse with equal care, that Rezon was an adversary not all the days of Solomon's life but all his days from his first going into idolatry to the end of it.
26:
Who Jeroboam was has to be settled against a rival identification and a misleading word. Gill reports that some Jewish writers made him the Sheba who had rebelled under David, and gives the two answers a rabbi returned: that man was of the tribe of Benjamin and this of Ephraim, and besides his head had been cut off and thrown over the wall to Joab. Ellicott corrects the description itself, since the word rendered Ephrathite usually means an inhabitant of Bethlehem but is here simply another form of Ephraimite; the town named he takes for a place of Ephraim in the Jordan valley, noting a Greek manuscript that reads a different name. The mention of the widowed mother, added to the description of him as Solomon's servant, he reads as designed to mark the utterly dependent condition from which the king's favour raised the future rebel. Henry makes the same detail kinder, that Providence had made up to the widow the loss of a husband in a son who was active and ingenious.

How he rose is a lesson Henry is glad to draw. It was Solomon's wisdom, when he had work to do, to employ proper persons in it; observing Jeroboam to be a very industrious young man, one that minded his business and took a pleasure in it and did it with all his might, he gradually advanced him until he was set over the burden of the house of Joseph. Industry is the way to preferment, Henry says: seest thou a man diligent in his business, one that will take care and pains and go through with it? He shall stand before kings. He then compares three reigns — when Saul saw a valiant man he took him to himself, when Solomon saw an industrious man he preferred him, but David's eyes were upon the faithful in the land. Ellicott deflates the title Jeroboam is given: the phrase about a mighty man of valour has nothing to do with war and simply signifies strong and capable, while the charge committed to him was the taskwork assigned to the levy from his own tribe.

Where the disaffection began is Clarke's contribution, and he locates it in a building site. Jeroboam was employed while a young man to superintend the works at Millo, and distinguished himself there so as to be set over all the labourers belonging to Ephraim and Manasseh. At first, Clarke says, Solomon employed none of the Israelites in any drudgery; but it is likely that as he grew profane he grew tyrannical and oppressive, and at the works of Millo he changed his conduct — and there in all probability were the seeds of disaffection sown, which so clever and enterprising a man knew well how to avail himself of. Ellicott supports the same reading from the chronology, that the building of Millo came after the Temple and the palace, some twenty years into the reign, when the delight in magnificence of building grew upon Solomon and with it the burdens of the people; he adds that the levy for the Temple, perhaps originally exceptional, had by now served as a precedent for laying burdens on Israelites and not merely on the subject races.
29:
The appearance of a prophet at this point is itself the event, and Ellicott says why. In the person of Ahijah, prophecy emerges from the abeyance which seems to overshadow it during the greatness of the monarchy. Even in David's old age Nathan appears chiefly as a counsellor and servant of the king, and from the day of the coronation we hear nothing of any prophetic action: Solomon himself receives the visions of the Lord, upon him as the Wise Man rests the special inspiration, and at the consecration of the Temple he alone is prominent as the representative and teacher of the people. Now, however, we find in Ahijah the first of a line of prophets who resumed a paramount influence like that of Samuel or Nathan, protecting the spirituality of the land and the worship of God, and demanding from king and people alike submission to the authority of the Lord. Clarke adds a biographical note, that Ahijah was one of those who wrote the history of Solomon's reign, and that it is supposed to have been by him that God spoke twice to Solomon and delivered the sentence earlier in this chapter.

When the meeting took place matters for the sense of the whole passage, and Keil and Delitzsch fix it. At that time means the time when Jeroboam had become overseer over the heavy works, not a time after he had already stirred up the rebellion; for the entire account that follows forms part of the explanation of the earlier statement that he lifted up his hand against the king. On his errand out of the city Gill offers two guesses, either that he was going to enter upon his new office or that he was returning to the country after paying in the revenues and making up his accounts; Clarke declines to guess at all, saying simply that on what errand he was going we do not know.

Whose garment was torn is a small question with a clear answer. Gill notes that the wording looks as if it were Jeroboam's, newly got to appear before the king in, though the sense may be that the prophet took hold of his own. Ellicott treats it as Ahijah's own and places the act in a series: symbolical acts are frequent in later prophecy, often alternating with symbolical visions and parables, and their object is to arrest attention and call out the inquiry, wilt thou not tell us what these things are to us? The rending of the garment here, he adds, is used exactly as Saul's rending of Samuel's mantle had been used, to symbolise the rending away of the kingdom. Keil and Delitzsch let the message itself supply the ground: the tribes are given away because the people have forsaken God and worshipped the goddess of the Zidonians, the god of the Moabites and the god of the Ammonites, and have not walked in his ways as did David.
34:
The arithmetic of the torn garment is spelled out by Clarke piece by piece. The garment was the symbol of the kingdom, the twelve pieces the symbol of the twelve tribes, and the ten given to Jeroboam the symbol of the ten tribes which should afterwards form the kingdom of Israel ruling in Samaria, to distinguish it from the kingdom of Judah ruling in Jerusalem. Gill reads the ten the same way and then has to account for the remainder, which he does by reckoning Judah and Benjamin as one tribe; and he marks the point at which the loss falls, that the kingdom is not taken out of Solomon's hand but out of his son's.

What the single tribe is reserved for is where the passage looks furthest forward. Gill offers three senses of the promise that David should have a light alway before God in Jerusalem, the city chosen to put his name there: a kingdom, as one old version renders it; or an illustrious prince and successor, shining in royal majesty to guide and direct and comfort the people; or an honour to David's family and a means of continuing the pure worship of God in the temple at Jerusalem. Clarke reduces it to one: that David's posterity may never fail and the regal line never become extinct, which he takes as a reference to the Messiah — who was not only David's light, he adds, but a light to enlighten the Gentiles.

What Jeroboam himself wanted is inferred by Clarke from a single clause of the promise. The words about all that his soul desired show, he says, that Jeroboam had already affected the kingdom and was seeking an opportunity to seize on the government; and God now tells him by his prophet what he shall have and what he shall not have, in order to prevent him from attempting to seize the whole kingdom to the prejudice of the spiritual seed of David. Gill keeps to the plain sense of the opening words, that God would take him from the low estate he was in and make him king.
38:
The promise made to Jeroboam is conditional, and both commentators on it note how the condition was answered. Keil and Delitzsch set out its terms as they stand: if he will hearken and walk in God's ways and keep his statutes as David did, then God will be with him and build him a sure house as he built for David, and give Israel to him. Clarke supplies what became of it — God would have continued his posterity on the throne of Israel had he not by his wickedness forfeited the promises and thrown himself out of the protection of the Most High.

The affliction promised to the house of David is limited in the same breath, and the limitation is what the witnesses seize. Gill states the cause plainly, the idolatry Solomon had been guilty of and connived at. Clarke reads the closing words as a horizon rather than a reprieve: the seed of David shall be in affliction and distress until the Messiah come, who shall sit on David's throne to order it and establish it in judgment and justice for ever; and he quotes a rabbi to the same effect, that when the Messiah comes the kingdom shall be restored to the house of David.

That Jeroboam actually rebelled is treated as established, and Keil and Delitzsch will not let the prophecy excuse it. The account of the flight continues the earlier statement that he lifted up his hand against the king, the intervening verses being simply an explanation of that statement; so it is obvious that he organised a rebellion, and equally obvious, from the sequence, that he did so only after the prophet had foretold his reigning over ten tribes when Solomon was dead — which, they insist, did not justify the attempt. Ellicott agrees and adds a motive on each side: the mere knowledge of the promise would be enough to excite the jealousy of the old king and incite him to try to falsify it by killing Jeroboam, while Jeroboam, characteristically enough, had not the patience to wait for its fulfilment and sought by some overt act to clutch at royalty — the Greek addition describing him as collecting three hundred chariots and assuming royal pretensions. Gill calls the attempted murder another instance of Solomon's folly, since he had himself been assured that the kingdom should be rent away and given to his servant; Clarke says he thought by this means to prevent the punishment due to his crimes.

The king he fled to is named, and the naming is itself evidence. Clarke observes that this is the first time we meet the proper name of an Egyptian king, Pharaoh being the common title of all the sovereigns of that country, and rejects the identification of Shishak with the conqueror renowned in Greek history, who he thinks lived long before Solomon's time. Ellicott identifies him confidently with a king of the Egyptian monuments whose accession the Egyptian traditions fix at about nine hundred and eighty years before Christ, and calls the identification an important point in Biblical chronology. He then turns the omission of the usual title into a proof of accuracy: the generic name Pharaoh is not given to Shishak here because he was not of the old royal line but the founder of a new dynasty, several of whose names are believed to have a Semitic origin arguing foreign extraction.
41:
The chapter ends as reigns end, with a reference, a figure, and a grave. Gill weighs three possibilities for the book of the acts of Solomon: written by the king himself, as Kimchi suggested, though not now in being; compiled by a chronologer Solomon employed to record the memorable events of his reign; or assembled out of several prophets. Henry takes the middle option, a court historiographer whose annals the inspired writer quarried for what God saw fit to transmit to the church. Clarke settles it from 2 Chronicles 9:29, where the acts stand in the book of Nathan, the prophecy of Ahijah the Shilonite, and the visions of Iddo the seer; from these, he supposes, both Kings and Chronicles were composed, and the originals are long since lost. Ellicott presses the same verse further, reading the prophets in the character of annalists and apportioning the reign among them: Nathan's book presumably covering only the early years, Ahijah's well able to cover most of the later reign, Iddo's visions touching the closing acts incidentally at best. He adds that Kings is itself visibly a compilation, differing from part to part in style and in degree of detail, the temple building and dedication coming from some temple record, the notes on territory and administration looking like extracts from official archives.

Forty years is the figure, and it draws more dispute than one might expect. Gill cites Eupolemus, a heathen writer, who allowed Solomon only fifty-two years of life; that suits the common Jewish tradition of accession at twelve, which Gill refutes from the age of Rehoboam. Josephus at the other extreme gives eighty years of reign and ninety-four of life, which Clarke calls sufficiently absurd and Ellicott ascribes either to an error in his Hebrew text or to a confusing together of the two reigns. Clarke prefers Calmet, eighteen at accession and death at fifty-eight, and adds grimly that given the excess in which the king lived this life was as long as could reasonably be expected. Keil and Delitzsch observe only that he was not more than twenty when he ascended the throne and so did not live to a very great age. Ellicott finds the exact equality with David's forty years curious, but refuses the easy inference: the accurate historical character of the whole narrative forbids treating such figures as round numbers signifying long duration.

Keil and Delitzsch raise here the question the older commentators argued at length, whether Solomon turned again to the Lord with all his heart, and leave it where Scripture leaves it, unascertainable. They allow one consideration on the hopeful side: if the leading thoughts of Ecclesiastes are traceable to him, we should have in that fact evidence of his conversion, or at least proof that he discovered at the close how empty earthly possessions and aims are, and named the fear of God the one abiding good by which a man can stand. Henry is gentler than the question deserves and no less severe in his summary. Solomon followed his fathers to the grave and was buried with honour in David's burying-place, and his son followed him to the throne, so that the graves fill with the generation going off while the houses fill with the one coming up. His reign was as long as his father's, but his life was not. Sin shortened his days.
43:
Gill's whole note on the last verse is that Solomon died as his fathers did. Clarke uses the same words to open five thousand of his own, an essay on the character of the king that is the longest thing in the chapter and the frankest. He died almost in the flower of his age, and, it appears, unregretted; his government was no blessing to Israel, and by its exactions laid the foundation of the schism that followed. Then Clarke sets out both sides in order. On the bright side: the boy was loved by the Lord and given by divine authority the name Jedidiah, beloved of the Lord, exchanged later for the peaceable name that matched both the quiet of the country and his own mild mind. He honoured his father's dying charge about the temple, though Clarke thinks the architectural knowledge was Hiram's and his workmen's rather than his own. He learned commerce from the Tyrians by sending his ships in company with theirs and taking their sailors aboard his own, a skill his quarrelling successors let dwindle until Israel could manage only a few boats on its inland lakes. His early piety was real: the prayer for wisdom and the prayer at the dedication put that beyond dispute. Of a thousand and five poems only the Song survives, which Clarke rates very high as literature and thinks has been allegorized to destruction; the natural history is wholly lost, and the East still repeats traditions of his seal and ring that have been so blended with fable that the precious can no longer be told from the vile.

Then the reverse. Clarke calls Solomon a man in whom everything great and everything mean predominated by turns, and lists the ways he forsook the God of his mercies. The affinity with Pharaoh's daughter was against the law whatever its politics, and Clarke believes it the first means of drawing his heart away. The expensive building obliged him to tax oppressively, the more so because the house of the forest of Lebanon consumed nearly thirteen years against the temple's seven. His reign opened inauspiciously with the death of Adonijah, which Clarke will not let state policy excuse. Seven hundred wives may be defended as alliance; the three hundred concubines cannot. And the idolatry followed as the law had warned it would, with a shrine for each foreign worship, until the light of God had gone out of that mind altogether. Clarke traces the taxation forward to the separation, the wars, and at length the captivity and the vanished ten tribes, and refuses the comfortable conjecture that Ecclesiastes proves a late repentance. The text that reports the apostasy reports the death, with no word of turning between them.
